newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY FINMIN SAYS GOVT TORN OVER ENERGY HIKE.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY FINMIN SAYS GOVT TORN OVER ENERGY HIKE.

text.p: Hungarian Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy told an economic forum on Friday that the government had to consider other interest groups than Western investors when fixing energy price rises for January.
"The government is in a difficult position," he said. "It has other interests to consider and should not be blamed for considering not only the investors but also consumers and Hungarian industry."

The government on Thursday announced retail hikes of 24.5 percent for electricity and 18.8 percent for gas but did not define the margins which would be granted to energy producers and distributors, in which Western utilities invested over $2 billion dollars last year.

Companies such as Gaz de France and German electricity giant RWE were promised an eight-per-cent return on investment from January 1996 and have expressed concern that the consumer hikes would be too small to generate such profits.
An Hungarian Energy Office (MEH) official told Reuters on Friday that the government would not announce the distribution of the price increases within the energy sector until mid-December.
Medgyessy assured investors that the eight percent profit margin had been built in to the rise but expressed reservations about its size.
"I was wondering whether the eight percent profit (so soon) is not rather high," he said.
But he warned Western investors not to look to the government to create its profits.

"Profit is not generated by the state, otherwise privatisation would not have been considered necessary," he said, adding that although the investors may be disappointed the decision was a "great step forward".
"The western investors will not be too enthusiastic but they will be encouraged that the government is meeting its obligations," he said.

Earlier, speaking at the same forum, Prime Minister Gyula Horn defended the government's handling of the energy price hike, which is intended to bring Hungarian rates more in line with those in the rest of Europe.

"I can safely say that our decision taken yesterday means that for the first time in Hungary prices will be proportional to costs with respect to energy and fuels and for the first time the energy sector will make a profit," Horn said.
